title: Why We Build the Breeder First
lede: Kronos builds the breeder (Hyperion) before the burner because a compact D-T machine reaches useful output on fusion gain alone.
body: Kronos develops two machines: a breeder (Hyperion), a compact D-T spherical tokamak, and a burner (Aegis / MetroVolt), a D-3He tandem-mirror generator. The breeder is built first. The reason is a difference in what each machine must demonstrate before it delivers value.

The breeder is an isotope and neutron foundry. Its product is material: a tritium class output near 4 kg/yr, a helium-3 coproduct near 1.97 kg/yr, and 14 MeV neutrons for irradiation services. To deliver those products the machine needs fusion gain, not net electrical output. A device with Q_sci of 3.076 producing 85.0 MW of fusion power generates the neutron flux that drives breeding and activation. That flux is the product.
Gain-only is a lower bar than net electric

Net electricity requires that recirculating power for magnets, heating, cryogenics, and balance-of-plant be smaller than gross electrical output. That is a harder threshold than scientific gain. The burner is designed toward net electric output via direct energy conversion, and its economics only close at fleet scale. Building it first would mean waiting on the harder demonstration before any value is delivered.

The breeder is sized to a supply requirement, not to a megawatt target. It is deliberately compact. That keeps the first build tractable, retires physics and engineering risk on the smaller machine, and produces a marketable output stream from the neutron economy while the burner physics continue to mature. The breeder also supplies the tritium and, over time, the helium-3 that the D-3He burner will eventually consume.
This page describes a design and simulation study, not a built machine. Construction begins Q2 2027; first-of-a-kind first tritium is targeted near 2030.

title: A Foundry, Not a Power Plant
lede: Hyperion is sized to an isotope supply requirement rather than an electrical output target; its product is material, not megawatts.
body: Sized to supply, not to output

Conventional fusion programs size a machine to a power rating and then ask whether the economics of selling that power close. Hyperion inverts the question. It is sized to the neutron flux needed to breed a target quantity of tritium and to activate materials for irradiation services. The output metric is kilograms per year and neutron-hours, not net megawatts.
14 MeV neutron flux for materials irradiation and isotope production

Because the product is material, the machine only needs fusion gain (Q_sci 3.076, 85.0 MW fusion power) to be useful. It does not need to clear the net-electric threshold. That removes the largest single physics-and-engineering dependency from the first build and lets the program deliver value from the neutron economy while the burner matures separately.

A foundry is defined by throughput, availability, and reproducibility of its output, not by peak rating. The engineering priorities follow: a reliable tritium plant, a breeding blanket tuned across breeding ratios of 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8, robust neutron handling, and maintainability for high duty. These priorities shape the assembly sequence, the diagnostics, and the gate program more than any single power number does.

Hyperion is a design and simulation study today. The foundry framing sets the acceptance criteria the first-of-a-kind unit must meet: sustained gain, a closed and accountable fuel loop, and a product stream that reproduces from unit to unit.

title: The Gain-Only Requirement
lede: Hyperion must reach fusion gain to deliver its products; it does not need to cross the harder net-electric threshold.
body: Scientific gain (Q_sci) is the ratio of fusion power produced to heating power injected into the plasma. Engineering gain, or net electric, additionally requires that total plant electrical draw, magnets, cryoplant, heating, pumps, controls, be smaller than gross electrical generation. These are different bars, and the gap between them is large.

Hyperion targets Q_sci of 3.076 with 85.0 MW of fusion power. At that operating point the 14 MeV neutron flux is sufficient to breed tritium and activate materials, which is the product. No conversion of fusion energy to net electricity is required for the foundry to function. The machine needs gain; it does not need net power.
Why the distinction matters for building first

Removing the net-electric requirement removes a chain of dependencies: high-efficiency conversion, minimized recirculating load, and the balance-of-plant scale that only pays off at large size. The breeder can therefore be compact and can be built and commissioned on a shorter path. The burner, by contrast, is designed toward net electric output through direct energy conversion, and its case closes only at fleet scale.
Q_sci is a plasma-physics ratio; net electric is a whole-plant ratio
Foundry products depend on neutron flux, which follows from gain
No hardware net-gain claim is made before the first-of-a-kind unit

This is a design and simulation study. The gain-only framing is what makes a near-term first build credible, and it is stated honestly: gain is claimed as a design point, not as demonstrated hardware performance.

title: Construction Begins Q2 2027
lede: Ground and long-lead procurement for the first-of-a-kind breeder are scheduled to begin in the second quarter of 2027.
body: The program schedule places the start of first-of-a-kind (FOAK) construction in Q2 2027. This is the transition from a design and simulation study to a physical build: site preparation, long-lead procurement of the superconducting magnet materials, and the start of vessel and structural fabrication.
What has to be true to start
A frozen design point: Q_sci 3.076, 85.0 MW, 9.66 MA plasma current, 16.84 T peak field
A licensing pathway under a byproduct-material framework in pre-application engagement
Committed magnet conductor supply and a qualified fabrication route
A site selected against neutron-handling, utility, and logistics criteria

The pacing items are the high-field magnets and the vacuum vessel. REBCO conductor procurement, coil winding, and structural fabrication have lead times measured in many months, so procurement begins at or near the start of construction even though installation comes later in the sequence. The Q2 2027 date is set by when those long-lead commitments can be responsibly placed.

Construction beginning is not the same as operation. The build is planned as roughly a 3.5-year path to the first unit, with first tritium targeted near 2030. Until the machine is assembled, commissioned, and taken through its physics gates, all performance figures remain design and simulation values.

title: The 3.5-Year Build to First Unit
lede: From Q2 2027 groundbreaking to first tritium, the first-of-a-kind breeder is planned on a roughly three-and-a-half-year path.
body: The first-of-a-kind (FOAK) breeder is planned on a build of roughly 3.5 years, from construction start in Q2 2027 to first tritium near 2030. The duration reflects a compact spherical tokamak with a demanding but bounded set of components, not a large power station.
Site preparation and civil works, in parallel with long-lead magnet and vessel procurement
Component fabrication: magnets, vacuum vessel, blanket modules, divertor, cryoplant
Assembly and integration in sequence around the centerpost and vessel
Commissioning: vacuum, cryogenic, magnet energization, then plasma
Why 3.5 years is plausible for FOAK

Compactness helps. A spherical tokamak concentrates the hardest engineering in the centerpost and central solenoid region, which shortens some structural spans and reduces total material relative to a large aspect-ratio device. The gain-only requirement removes balance-of-plant needed for net electric conversion. The schedule is nonetheless a first-of-a-kind estimate; later NOAK and BOAK units are planned to build faster as procurement and assembly mature.

No unit is built yet. The 3.5-year figure is a plan, not an achievement, and it depends on magnet supply, licensing timing, and assembly execution proceeding as designed. The program states schedule risk openly and retires it through the gate program rather than assuming it away.

title: FOAK First Tritium ~2030
lede: The first-of-a-kind breeder targets its first bred tritium around 2030, the milestone that proves the foundry function end to end.
body: First tritium is the milestone that matters most for a breeder. It means the machine has produced fusion neutrons, those neutrons have bred tritium in the blanket, and the tritium plant has recovered and accounted for it. First tritium is targeted around 2030 for the first-of-a-kind (FOAK) unit.
Sustained D-T plasma at or near the design gain point
A neutron flux consistent with 85.0 MW-class fusion power
A breeding blanket that converts neutrons to tritium at a measured breeding ratio
A fuel loop that recovers, measures, and accounts for bred tritium
Why it is the product proof, not a power proof

First tritium proves the foundry, not net electricity. It shows the neutron economy works: neutrons are produced, captured, and converted to a saleable isotope stream. It does not claim net power, and none is claimed before FOAK. The distinction is deliberate and stated plainly throughout the program.

First tritium will be reported against pre-registered predictions for neutron yield and breeding ratio, so the demonstrated value can be compared to the design point rather than presented on its own. The design point today, breeding ratio treated as a lever across 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8, and products near 4 kg/yr tritium class plus 1.97 kg/yr helium-3, is a simulation result until first tritium confirms it on hardware.

title: FOAK to NOAK to BOAK
lede: The breeder program is a sequence: first-of-a-kind proves the machine, then nth-of-a-kind and best-of-a-kind units standardize and improve it.
body: The breeder is built as a short series rather than a one-off. The first-of-a-kind (FOAK) unit proves the physics and the foundry function. Nth-of-a-kind (NOAK) units apply the lessons of the first build. Best-of-a-kind (BOAK) units standardize the design for repeatable manufacture.

FOAK carries the physics risk. Its job is to reach gain, breed tritium, and validate the design point against pre-registered predictions. It is expected to be the slowest to build and the most heavily instrumented, because its purpose is measurement and risk retirement.

NOAK units incorporate what FOAK teaches: assembly steps that took too long, components that underperformed, diagnostics that proved unnecessary or missing. NOAK is where build time and reliability improve while the design point stays essentially fixed.

BOAK is the settled design intended for repeatable fabrication and predictable output. At this stage the machine is a manufactured product with known lead times and known performance, suited to running as a foundry with high availability.
FOAK retires physics and integration risk
NOAK retires build and operability risk
BOAK locks the standard for a small foundry fleet

The whole sequence remains a plan. FOAK is not yet built. The learning-curve framing describes how the program intends to move from a single demonstrated machine to a small, reproducible foundry fleet without overclaiming at any step.

title: The Gate Program
lede: Three physics gates, confinement, magnet, and fuel loop, structure how the breeder retires its largest risks before claiming its design point.
body: The breeder program organizes risk retirement into discrete gates. Each gate is a defined demonstration with a pre-registered prediction and a pass criterion. A gate is passed when measured hardware performance meets the prediction, not when a model says it should. This keeps claims tied to evidence.
G1 Confinement: the plasma holds energy long enough to reach the design gain point
G2 Magnet: the high-field magnet system reaches and holds 16.84 T peak field under load
G3 Fuel loop: neutrons breed tritium and the fuel cycle recovers and accounts for it
How gates relate to the schedule

The gates are sequenced with commissioning. Magnet energization (toward G2) precedes plasma; confinement (G1) is demonstrated once plasma operation begins; the fuel loop (G3) is proven at first tritium. Passing all three is what turns the first-of-a-kind unit from an assembled machine into a demonstrated foundry.

Each gate has predictions registered before the test, covering the quantities the gate is meant to prove: energy confinement time, achieved field, neutron yield, and breeding ratio. Reporting measured against predicted, rather than reporting the measurement alone, is how the program distinguishes a genuine demonstration from a retrofit explanation.

The gates apply to a machine that is not yet built. They are the acceptance structure for the first build, and every design-point number cited elsewhere on this site remains a simulation value until the relevant gate is passed.

title: G1: The Confinement Gate
lede: The first gate proves the plasma confines energy well enough to reach the design gain point of Q_sci 3.076.
body: G1 is the confinement gate. It demonstrates that the plasma holds its thermal energy long enough, at the design current and field, to reach the target gain. Confinement is quantified by the energy confinement time and its scaling with plasma current, density, and heating power.

The design point is Q_sci 3.076 at 85.0 MW fusion power, with 9.66 MA of plasma current in a negative-triangularity (delta -0.30) spherical configuration. G1 is passed when the plasma sustains the confinement required to hold that operating point long enough to produce the neutron flux the foundry needs.

The chosen delta of -0.30 is intended to manage edge behavior and heat exhaust while preserving core confinement. G1 tests whether the predicted confinement holds at the real triangularity and current, since edge and core physics interact in ways that simulation can only bound, not settle.
Measured quantity: energy confinement time at design current and field
Pass criterion: confinement sufficient to reach the Q_sci 3.076 operating point
Registered prediction: confinement time and its uncertainty band, filed before the test

Confinement scaling is the least certain part of any tokamak design. G1 is placed first because it carries the most physics risk. Until G1 is passed on the built machine, Q_sci 3.076 is a design and simulation value, and the program says so.

title: G2: The Magnet Gate
lede: The second gate proves the high-field magnet system reaches and holds 16.84 T peak field with 8 T on axis under operational load.
body: G2 is the magnet gate. It demonstrates that the superconducting magnet system reaches the design fields, 16.84 T peak at the conductor with 8 T on axis, and holds them stably under the mechanical and thermal loads of operation. Field is what confines the plasma; without it there is no gain.

High field in a compact spherical tokamak concentrates enormous stress in the centerpost and toroidal-field structure. The magnet must carry current density high enough to produce 16.84 T while withstanding Lorentz forces and staying superconducting under quench-protected conditions. This is the hardest engineering test in the machine.
Measured quantity: achieved peak field and on-axis field under load
Pass criterion: 16.84 T peak / 8 T on axis, held stably through an operational cycle
Registered prediction: field, conductor temperature margin, and quench behavior

G2 is demonstrated during commissioning, before full plasma operation, because the field must be proven before the plasma that depends on it. Magnet energization, temperature-margin verification, and controlled quench testing are part of the gate. Only after the magnet holds design field is the machine cleared to pursue G1 confinement at the full operating point.

The magnet is a design informed by REBCO high-temperature superconductor practice, but the specific coil set is not yet built. G2 is where conductor supply, winding quality, and structural design meet reality. The 16.84 T figure is a design target until the gate is passed.

title: G3: The Fuel Loop Gate
lede: The third gate proves neutrons breed tritium in the blanket and the fuel cycle recovers, measures, and accounts for it.
body: G3 is the fuel loop gate and coincides with first tritium. It demonstrates the full breeding chain: fusion neutrons enter the blanket, breed tritium in lithium-bearing material, and the tritium plant recovers, measures, and accounts for the product. G3 is the proof that Hyperion functions as a foundry.

Tritium breeding ratio (TBR) is treated as a design lever, studied across values of 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8. TBR above 1.0 means the blanket breeds more tritium than the plasma consumes, the condition for a self-sustaining and product-yielding fuel cycle. G3 measures the achieved TBR against the registered prediction for the installed blanket.
Measured quantity: neutron yield, achieved TBR, and recovered tritium mass
Pass criterion: closed, accounted fuel loop with TBR consistent with the design lever
Registered prediction: neutron yield and TBR with uncertainty, filed before the test

A breeder must account for every gram of tritium for both product and regulatory reasons. G3 therefore includes demonstrating the measurement and accountancy system, not just producing tritium. Recovery efficiency and inventory tracking are part of the pass criterion.

There is an open reconciliation between a design-level TBR of 1.8 and the net breeding available in a real three-dimensional blanket with penetrations and structure. G3 is precisely where that reconciliation is settled by measurement. Until then, product figures near 4 kg/yr tritium class remain design values.

title: Pre-Registered Predictions
lede: Before each gate, the program files the numbers it expects to measure, so demonstrations are judged against commitments rather than hindsight.
body: Pre-registration means writing down the predicted result of a test, with its uncertainty, before the test is run. The breeder program applies this discipline to every physics gate. The value is simple: a prediction filed in advance cannot be adjusted after the fact to match whatever the machine did.
G1: energy confinement time and the resulting Q_sci at design current and field
G2: achieved peak field, conductor temperature margin, and quench behavior
G3: neutron yield, tritium breeding ratio, and recovered tritium mass

Fusion has a long history of results explained after the fact. Reporting measured-versus-predicted, with both numbers visible, lets outside reviewers see whether the design models actually predicted the machine, or only rationalized it. It also makes a miss informative: a confinement time below prediction tells the program exactly where the model was wrong.

A pre-registered prediction that the machine fails to meet is not hidden. It is reported, and it feeds directly into the NOAK design revision. The program treats a documented miss on FOAK as the intended function of a first-of-a-kind unit: to find where reality departs from simulation while the stakes are contained.

All current numbers, Q_sci 3.076, 16.84 T, TBR across 1.1/1.5/1.8, are predictions in this sense. They are simulation-based design values, registered as the targets the built machine will be measured against.

title: What Each Gate Proves
lede: A compact map of the breeder gate program: the physics each gate settles, and the risk each one retires.
body: The three physics gates are not interchangeable. Each isolates one dominant uncertainty so it can be settled independently, in the order that the machine can demonstrate it.
G1 Confinement / Plasma holds energy to reach Q_sci 3.076 / Confinement-scaling risk
G2 Magnet / 16.84 T peak, 8 T on axis, held under load / High-field magnet and structural risk
G3 Fuel loop / Neutrons breed and are accounted as tritium / Breeding and fuel-cycle risk

G1 addresses whether the plasma physics deliver the design gain. G2 addresses whether the enabling magnet technology is real at the required field. G3 addresses whether the neutron economy closes into a product. Only with all three passed is the foundry demonstrated end to end.
What the gates deliberately do not prove
Net electric output, which the breeder does not target
Fleet-scale reproducibility, which is NOAK and BOAK work
Burner physics, which are a separate machine and program

Magnet before plasma, plasma before fuel loop. Each gate depends on the one before it: no field, no confinement; no confinement, no neutrons; no neutrons, no bred tritium. The sequence mirrors the physical dependencies of the machine and the commissioning order.
Every entry above is a target for a machine not yet built. The gates are how those targets become demonstrated results.

title: Manufacturing Plan
lede: The breeder is designed for fabrication, with the hardest components, magnets and vessel, treated as long-lead manufactured items from the start.
body: A machine intended to become a small foundry fleet must be manufacturable, not just buildable once. The breeder design separates components into standard fabricated assemblies so that FOAK experience transfers directly to NOAK and BOAK production.
High-field magnets: REBCO conductor procurement, coil winding, and structural casing
Vacuum vessel: precision-fabricated, low-outgassing structure sized to the compact geometry
Breeding blanket modules: lithium-bearing assemblies designed for replacement
Centerpost: the mechanically and thermally loaded core of a spherical tokamak

Magnet conductor and the vessel dominate the schedule, so their procurement begins at the start of construction in Q2 2027 even though installation is later. Treating them as long-lead items from day one is what makes the roughly 3.5-year FOAK build achievable.

FOAK components are expected to be partly bespoke. The manufacturing plan captures which steps were slow, which tolerances were hard to hold, and which parts should be standardized. NOAK converts those lessons into repeatable fabrication, and BOAK settles the standard so that a small number of near-identical machines can be produced with known lead times.
This plan describes intended fabrication for a machine not yet built. It contains no cost content; it is about sequence, lead time, and reproducibility.

title: Supply Chain
lede: The breeder depends on a small number of critical supply lines, high-field superconductor, lithium-bearing blanket materials, and tritium-handling systems.
body: A compact D-T breeder concentrates its supply risk in a few materials and systems. Securing them is a precondition for the Q2 2027 construction start, because their lead times set the schedule.
REBCO high-temperature superconductor for the high-field magnets
Lithium-bearing materials for the breeding blanket
Tritium-handling and accountancy systems for the fuel loop
Specialized vacuum, cryogenic, and neutron-shielding components

REBCO conductor availability and qualification are the tightest constraint. The 16.84 T peak field depends on it, and global manufacturing capacity for high-quality tape is finite. The program treats conductor supply as a committed, qualified route before construction begins rather than an open procurement.

Breeding performance depends on lithium isotopics and blanket geometry. The supply plan covers lithium-bearing material and the neutron multipliers and structure that set the achievable breeding ratio across the 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8 lever range.

Tritium systems, recovery, storage, and accountancy, are specialized and regulated. They are procured and qualified in step with the licensing pathway so the fuel loop can be operated and accounted for at first tritium.
Supply-chain readiness is a build precondition, not an operational detail. This page describes intended sourcing for a machine not yet built and contains no pricing or cost content.

title: REBCO Magnet Supply
lede: High-field operation at 16.84 T depends on REBCO high-temperature superconductor, the single most constrained item in the build.
body: Reaching 16.84 T peak field in a compact spherical tokamak requires high-temperature superconductor. REBCO (rare-earth barium copper oxide) tape carries the current density needed at high field and elevated temperature margin, which is why it anchors the magnet design and the schedule.

REBCO tape is manufactured by a limited set of producers, and the quantity and quality needed for a full toroidal-field magnet set are substantial. Conductor procurement is therefore a long-lead commitment placed at the start of construction, and conductor qualification, verifying current-carrying performance and defect rates, is part of accepting the supply.
Procure and qualify conductor tape against current-density and defect criteria
Wind and insulate coils to hold tolerance under high field
Assemble the structural casing that carries Lorentz loads
Integrate quench protection to keep the magnet within temperature margin

The magnet is proven at gate G2: the coil set must reach and hold 16.84 T peak with 8 T on axis under operational load. REBCO supply quality feeds directly into whether G2 passes, which is why conductor qualification is treated as rigorously as the field test itself.

The magnet is a design informed by REBCO practice; the specific coil set is not yet built. Author reconciliation on some REBCO material details is tracked as an open item in the program's documentation.

title: Siting the First Unit
lede: The first-of-a-kind breeder is sited against neutron-handling, utility, logistics, and regulatory criteria rather than against a power-market location.
body: Because the breeder is a foundry, not a power plant, siting is driven by the needs of a neutron and isotope facility, not by proximity to an electricity market. The dominant criteria are radiological handling, utility supply for magnets and cryogenics, and logistics for heavy long-lead components.
Radiological siting suitable for 14 MeV neutron work and tritium handling
Electrical supply adequate for magnet energization and cryoplant load
Cooling water and utilities for the cryogenic and vacuum systems
Transport access for the vessel, magnets, and heavy assemblies
A regulatory environment compatible with a byproduct-material framework

Neutron shielding, activation management, and tritium containment set the site footprint and building design. The facility is designed around confining neutrons and accounting for tritium, which places the shielding and the tritium plant at the center of the layout.

The vessel, centerpost, and magnet assemblies are large, heavy, and precision items. Site access for their transport and installation is a real constraint, and it interacts with the assembly sequence: components must arrive in the order they are installed.
No site build has begun; site preparation is part of the Q2 2027 construction start. Siting criteria here describe intended selection factors for a machine not yet built.

title: Licensing Under a Byproduct-Material Framework
lede: The breeder pursues licensing through a byproduct-material framework suited to a device that produces isotopes and neutrons rather than grid power.
body: Matching the framework to the machine

Regulatory frameworks were built for the machines regulators knew. A fusion breeder that produces isotopes and neutrons, and handles tritium, fits more naturally under a byproduct-material framework than under a large fission-reactor licensing regime. The program pursues licensing on that basis.

The hazards to be regulated are radioactive material handling, neutron activation, and tritium accountancy, precisely the domain of byproduct-material regulation. The machine does not present the accident spectrum of a fission core, and its product is material, which aligns the regulatory question with how the facility actually behaves.
Neutron activation and shielding of the facility and components
Radioactive material handling, storage, and transport
Worker and public dose management around a compact source

Rather than arriving with a finished application, the program engages regulators early through pre-application discussion, so the licensing basis is agreed as the design matures. This reduces the risk of late redesign and gives the regulator visibility into a machine type that is new to them.

The licensing pathway is in engagement, not approval. It is a precondition being worked in parallel with the Q2 2027 construction start, and counsel review governs formal submissions. The framework choice is described here as the intended pathway for a machine not yet built or licensed.

title: The Pre-Application Pathway
lede: Early, structured engagement with the regulator establishes the licensing basis before a formal application, reducing late-stage design risk.
body: The program favors pre-application engagement: structured discussion with the regulator well before a formal license application. For a machine type the regulator has not licensed before, this establishes shared understanding of the hazards, the framework, and the evidence the application will need to contain.
Which regulatory framework applies, a byproduct-material basis for this device
What the safety case must demonstrate for tritium, neutrons, and activation
What analyses and test evidence the eventual application will rely on
How the gate program's measurements support the licensing basis

The costliest licensing outcome is discovering late that the regulator expects a different basis or additional evidence, forcing redesign after construction has advanced. Pre-application surfaces those expectations while the design is still adjustable, aligning the build with the licensing basis rather than reconciling them at the end.

Pre-application runs in parallel with detailed design and the start of construction in Q2 2027. The physics gates produce evidence that feeds the licensing basis: neutron and tritium accountancy from G3, in particular, are directly relevant to a byproduct-material safety case.
This is engagement, not authorization. Formal submissions are governed by counsel review, and the pathway described here is the program's intended route for a machine not yet licensed.

title: Assembly Sequence
lede: The compact spherical tokamak is assembled from the centerpost outward, with the vessel, magnets, blanket, and diagnostics installed in dependency order.
body: A spherical tokamak concentrates its structure at the center, so assembly proceeds broadly from the centerpost and central column outward. The order is set by physical dependencies: each component must be installed before the ones that surround or connect to it.
Foundation and shielding structure at the selected site
Toroidal-field magnet assembly and vacuum vessel integration
Breeding blanket modules and divertor installation

Once the vessel is closed and the magnets are in place, interior access is limited. Blanket modules, the divertor, and internal diagnostics are therefore installed before final closure. Getting the sequence wrong forces disassembly, which is why the assembly plan is fixed and rehearsed before the first component arrives.

Heavy components, the vessel, magnets, and centerpost, must arrive in installation order. This couples the assembly sequence to the supply chain and site logistics: a late long-lead item stalls everything downstream of it, which is why magnet and vessel procurement lead the schedule.
This describes the intended assembly of a machine not yet built. The sequence is a plan that the first-of-a-kind build will test and the manufacturing plan will refine for NOAK.

title: Commissioning Plan
lede: Commissioning brings the assembled breeder to life system by system, vacuum, cryogenics, magnets, then plasma, before the physics gates.
body: Commissioning is the staged bring-up of a fully assembled machine. Each subsystem is verified in isolation and then in combination, in an order that respects dependencies, before the machine is asked to make plasma or produce neutrons.
Vacuum: pump down and leak-check the vessel to operating pressure
Cryogenics: cool the magnets to operating temperature and verify margin
Magnets: energize toward 16.84 T and verify field and quench protection (feeds G2)
Plasma: first plasma at low parameters, then build toward the design point (feeds G1)
Fuel loop: D-T operation, breeding, and tritium recovery (feeds G3)

Commissioning has its own acceptance checks, vacuum quality, cryogenic stability, magnet energization, that are engineering milestones. The physics gates (G1, G2, G3) sit on top of these: G2 is reached during magnet commissioning, G1 during plasma operation, and G3 at first tritium. Passing commissioning is necessary but not sufficient; the physics gates are the real demonstration.

Commissioning is where integration problems surface, subsystems that worked alone but interact badly together. The plan expects and instruments for this. Until commissioning is complete and the gates are passed, all performance figures remain design and simulation values for a machine not yet operated.

title: First Plasma
lede: First plasma is the moment the commissioned breeder confines its first ionized fuel, the start of the path to the confinement gate.
body: First plasma is achieved when the machine, with magnets energized and vessel under vacuum, forms and confines its first plasma. It is a low-parameter event, far below the design operating point, but it confirms that the core systems work together: field, vacuum, fueling, and control.
The magnet system produces a confining field the plasma responds to
Vacuum and fueling systems deliver and hold the plasma
Plasma control and diagnostics function on a real discharge
The machine is integrated well enough to operate

First plasma is not gain, not the design current of 9.66 MA, and not neutron production at scale. It is the beginning of a ramp: from first plasma the program builds current, field, and heating toward the Q_sci 3.076 operating point, which is where the confinement gate G1 is judged.
From first plasma to the design point

The path from first plasma to full performance is incremental and heavily instrumented, so that each step is compared to the pre-registered predictions for confinement and gain. Problems found here, control instabilities, unexpected losses, are exactly what a first-of-a-kind machine is built to find.

First plasma follows commissioning and precedes the confinement gate. It is a planned milestone for a machine not yet built; no plasma performance is claimed as demonstrated until it is measured on hardware.

title: First Tritium as a Program Milestone
lede: First tritium is the single milestone that converts the breeder from a physics demonstrator into a working foundry.
body: Why first tritium defines the program

Every earlier milestone, first plasma, the confinement gate, the magnet gate, builds toward one result: bred, recovered, and accounted tritium. First tritium, targeted near 2030 for the first-of-a-kind unit, is where the machine first produces its actual product.
The full chain in one event

First tritium requires the entire foundry chain to work at once: sustained D-T plasma near the design gain, a neutron flux consistent with 85.0 MW-class fusion power, a blanket that breeds tritium at a measured ratio, and a fuel loop that recovers and accounts for it. It is the integration test of the whole concept.
Confirms the neutron economy closes into a saleable isotope stream
Validates the breeding blanket at real, three-dimensional geometry
Demonstrates tritium accountancy for product and regulatory purposes
Establishes the baseline for the ~4 kg/yr tritium-class output figure

First tritium is reported measured-versus-predicted for neutron yield and breeding ratio, per the pre-registration discipline. This is where the open reconciliation between a design TBR of 1.8 and real three-dimensional net breeding is settled by data rather than argument.
First tritium is a target, not an achievement. It sits at the end of the roughly 3.5-year FOAK build. Until it is measured, the product figures on this site are design and simulation values.

title: The Fleet Plan
lede: The breeder plan is a small number of foundry units, not a large power fleet; scale is set by isotope demand, not by megawatts.
body: The breeder is not planned as a growing fleet of power stations. It is planned as a small number of foundry units, enough to meet an isotope and neutron supply requirement. The fleet is sized to demand for tritium, helium-3, and neutron services, not to an energy market.

Each unit produces a tritium-class output near 4 kg/yr and a helium-3 coproduct near 1.97 kg/yr. A few units cover a large fraction of realistic near-term demand for these materials. Building more than the supply requires would serve no purpose, because the product is material with a bounded market, not electricity with open demand.
FOAK proves the machine and the foundry function
NOAK units apply build and operability lessons
BOAK standardizes the design for repeatable manufacture
The total fleet is set by isotope demand, not by capacity growth

The breeder foundry also supplies fuel to the future burner (Aegis / MetroVolt): tritium now, and helium-3 over time. The breeder fleet and the burner fleet are different in character, the breeder a small foundry, the burner a larger energy fleet gated on separate physics and on lunar helium-3 supply, and they are planned separately.
The fleet plan describes intended deployment of a machine not yet built. It carries no capacity or cost projections, only the supply-driven logic for keeping the breeder fleet small.

title: Foundry, Not Power Fleet
lede: The breeder fleet is measured in isotope output and neutron-hours, not installed capacity; it is an industrial source, not a utility.
body: A power fleet grows to meet electricity demand and is measured in installed capacity. A foundry fleet exists to supply a material and is measured in output per year. The breeder is the second kind. Confusing the two leads to the wrong questions about scale and purpose.
Tritium, the bankable base product, near 4 kg/yr per unit class
Helium-3 coproduct, near 1.97 kg/yr per unit
14 MeV neutrons for materials irradiation and isotope production

The breeder needs only fusion gain, not net electricity, and its economics rest on materials rather than megawatts. Scaling it into a power fleet would demand the net-electric threshold it is deliberately designed to avoid, and would size the fleet to an energy market it was never meant to serve. The burner is the machine designed toward energy at fleet scale.

Foundry operation prioritizes availability, reproducibility, and accountancy: keeping units running, producing consistent output unit to unit, and tracking every gram of tritium. These priorities shape maintenance design, diagnostics, and the fuel loop far more than any peak-power figure.

This describes intended operation of machines not yet built, and contains no economic figures. The distinction it draws, foundry versus power fleet, is the organizing idea behind why the breeder is built first and kept small.

title: Risk Retirement
lede: The build is organized to retire the largest physics and engineering risks in a defined order, with the first-of-a-kind unit as the primary risk-retirement instrument.
body: Rather than assuming the design is correct, the program identifies its largest uncertainties and retires them in sequence. The first-of-a-kind (FOAK) unit is the main instrument for this: its purpose is to convert the biggest simulation-based assumptions into measured results.
Confinement scaling: will the plasma reach Q_sci 3.076? (retired at G1)
High-field magnets: is 16.84 T real at scale under load? (retired at G2)
Breeding: does the blanket net-breed tritium in real 3-D geometry? (retired at G3)
Integration: do the subsystems work together? (retired in commissioning)
Build execution: can the machine be built in ~3.5 years? (retired by FOAK itself)

Some risks cannot be retired by more simulation, they require the built machine. FOAK is heavily instrumented and reported against pre-registered predictions precisely so that each measured result closes an open question. A FOAK that finds problems has done its job.

The program tracks specific open items honestly, including the reconciliation between design-level and net three-dimensional tritium breeding ratio, and details of the magnet materials. These are named, not hidden, and are mapped to the gates that will settle them.
Risk retirement describes a machine not yet built. Its honesty is the point: the program states what is unproven and where each unknown gets resolved.

title: Design and Simulation, Not Yet Built
lede: Every performance figure for the breeder is a design and simulation value today; no unit is built, and no hardware net-gain is claimed.
body: It is important to state plainly: Hyperion is a design and simulation study. No unit is built. Construction of the first-of-a-kind machine is scheduled to begin in Q2 2027, with first tritium targeted near 2030. Everything before that is design, analysis, and simulation.
What that means for the numbers
Q_sci 3.076 and 85.0 MW fusion power are design-point targets
16.84 T peak field and 9.66 MA plasma current are design values
TBR across 1.1/1.5/1.8 is a design lever, not a measured result
Products near 4 kg/yr tritium class and 1.97 kg/yr helium-3 are projected outputs

The program makes no claim of hardware net gain, and in fact the breeder does not target net electricity at all, only fusion gain. Any figure describing performance is a prediction to be tested at the gates, reported measured-versus-predicted.

Fusion has been harmed by overclaiming. Stating design-versus-built status clearly, on every relevant page, is how the program keeps its credibility. The value of the work is real, a rigorous design and a concrete build plan, but it is design, and calling it anything else would be dishonest.
When the machine is built and the gates are passed, these values become results. Until then, they are the targets the build is organized to meet.

title: Why a Spherical Tokamak
lede: The breeder uses a spherical (low aspect ratio) tokamak because it reaches high plasma pressure at accessible field and stays compact.
body: Hyperion is a spherical tokamak: a tokamak with a low aspect ratio, where the plasma is more nearly spherical than the classic doughnut shape. This choice follows directly from the foundry mission of reaching gain in a compact machine.
Higher plasma pressure (beta) for a given magnetic field, improving fusion output efficiency
Compact size, which shortens the build and concentrates the hard engineering
Strong plasma shaping, which supports the chosen negative triangularity

The spherical geometry concentrates stress and heat in a slender centerpost, which becomes the hardest engineering problem in the machine. The design accepts this trade because compactness and high beta serve the gain-only foundry mission better than a large, low-field conventional tokamak would.
How it shapes the rest of the design

The spherical choice drives the centerpost engineering, the high 16.84 T peak field, the 9.66 MA plasma current, and the negative triangularity of -0.30. These are not independent choices; they are a coherent set that follows from deciding to reach gain in a compact machine.

The configuration is a design decision for a machine not yet built. Its merits, high beta at accessible field, compactness, are the reasons the breeder can plausibly be the first machine Kronos builds.

title: The Compact-Machine Rationale
lede: A compact machine is chosen because a foundry is sized to supply, not to power, and small size shortens the build and concentrates risk.
body: Hyperion is deliberately compact. Since the mission is to supply a target quantity of isotopes and neutrons, not to generate a large amount of electricity, there is no reason to make the machine large. Compactness is an advantage for a foundry, not a compromise.
Less total material and fewer oversized components to procure
Concentrated engineering, most risk sits in the centerpost and magnets
A machine that can plausibly be built first, before the larger burner

High field does the work that size would otherwise do. A peak field of 16.84 T, enabled by REBCO superconductor, lets a small spherical tokamak reach the confinement and pressure needed for gain. The spherical geometry raises achievable plasma pressure for that field. Together they make a compact machine capable of Q_sci 3.076.

Compactness raises engineering stress. The centerpost carries high field, high current, and neutron loading in a small volume. This is the price of a small machine, and it is why centerpost engineering and the magnet gate G2 are central to the program.
The rationale describes a design choice for a machine not yet built. Compactness is what makes building the breeder first a credible plan rather than an aspiration.

title: The Breeding-Ratio Lever
lede: Tritium breeding ratio is treated as a design lever studied across 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8, not as a single fixed number.
body: Tritium breeding ratio (TBR) is the ratio of tritium bred in the blanket to tritium consumed by the plasma. The breeder treats TBR as a design lever, studied across 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8, rather than committing to a single value, because the achievable ratio depends on blanket design choices that trade against each other.
TBR 1.1: modest surplus, tighter blanket, less margin for penetrations
TBR 1.5: substantial surplus supporting product output and fuel self-sufficiency
TBR 1.8: high design-level surplus, most demanding blanket configuration

Real blankets have penetrations for heating, diagnostics, and maintenance, plus structure that absorbs neutrons. These reduce net breeding below the idealized figure. Studying a range makes the design honest about the gap between a one-dimensional design value and net three-dimensional performance, and lets the blanket be tuned to the product requirement.

There is a flagged reconciliation between a design-level TBR of 1.8 and the net breeding a real three-dimensional blanket delivers. The program does not paper over this. It is one of the specific items the fuel-loop gate G3 is designed to settle by measurement at first tritium.
TBR values here are design levers for a machine not yet built. The product figure near 4 kg/yr tritium class follows from the chosen point on this lever and remains a projection until G3.

title: Neutron Budget and Products
lede: The breeder's 14 MeV neutrons are a budget: some breed tritium, some make helium-3, and some serve materials irradiation.
body: In a breeder, the fusion neutrons are the product, not a byproduct. Each D-T fusion produces a 14 MeV neutron, and the machine's output at 85.0 MW fusion power is fundamentally a neutron flux that is then allocated to different uses.
Breeding: neutrons captured in the lithium-bearing blanket produce tritium (~4 kg/yr class)
Coproduction: pathways yield a helium-3 coproduct (~1.97 kg/yr)
Irradiation services: 14 MeV neutrons for materials testing and isotope production

A neutron used for one purpose is not available for another. Blanket coverage, penetrations, and multipliers all shift the budget. Framing output as a neutron budget makes the trade-offs explicit: raising breeding ratio, for example, may compete with neutron availability for irradiation services.

The tritium class output near 4 kg/yr is the bankable base product; helium-3 near 1.97 kg/yr is a strategically valuable coproduct; neutron-hours are a service. All three flow from the same 85.0 MW neutron source, which is why gain, not net power, is the requirement.
These are projected outputs for a machine not yet built. The actual budget is measured at the fuel-loop gate, where neutron yield and breeding ratio are reported against pre-registered predictions.

title: The Helium-3 Coproduct
lede: The breeder yields a helium-3 coproduct near 1.97 kg/yr, a strategically valuable material that also feeds the future D-3He burner.
body: Alongside its tritium-class output, the breeder produces a helium-3 coproduct near 1.97 kg/yr. Helium-3 is scarce and strategically valuable, with uses that make it important beyond its quantity. It is a coproduct of the same neutron economy that breeds tritium.

Helium-3 arises from the tritium pathway: tritium decays to helium-3, and the fuel cycle can recover it. This links the two products, tritium is the bankable base, and helium-3 accumulates from it, so the fuel loop is designed to recover and account for both.
Scarcity: terrestrial helium-3 supply is very limited
Strategic value distinct from revenue, its importance is not simply its mass
Fuel for the future burner: the D-3He burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) consumes helium-3
The strategic link to the burner

The breeder's helium-3 connects the two machines. The burner is a D-3He generator, and its fuel supply is a long-term constraint gated on lunar helium-3 availability. The breeder's coproduct is one terrestrial source in that picture, though the burner's fleet-scale needs are far larger. Helium-3's value here is framed as strategic, not as a revenue figure.
The 1.97 kg/yr figure is a design projection for a machine not yet built, recovered and confirmed only once the fuel loop operates.

title: Negative Triangularity
lede: The breeder plasma is shaped with negative triangularity of delta -0.30 to manage heat exhaust while preserving core confinement.
body: Triangularity describes the D-shape of the plasma cross-section. Negative triangularity turns the D outward, the reverse of the conventional inward shape. The breeder uses a negative triangularity of delta -0.30 as a canonical design choice.
Improved edge behavior, potentially avoiding certain edge instabilities
Favorable heat-exhaust characteristics for the divertor
Compatibility with the compact spherical geometry and its strong shaping capability

Negative triangularity is less conventional than positive, and its confinement and stability behavior at the design current and field is exactly what the confinement gate G1 must verify. The choice is made because its edge and exhaust benefits suit a compact high-field machine, but it places real demands on demonstrating core confinement at delta -0.30.
How it interacts with the machine

The shape does not stand alone. It is chosen together with the 9.66 MA plasma current, the 8 T on-axis field, and the compact spherical geometry so that core confinement and edge exhaust are balanced at the design gain point. The divertor design in particular is coupled to the triangularity, because the exhaust the divertor must handle depends on how the plasma edge is shaped.

The negative triangularity is canonical and must be represented consistently, the plasma D-shape opens outward. This matters in the machine's models and visualizations, where a triangularity of the wrong sign would misrepresent the design. The program tracks correct triangularity depiction as a documentation requirement, and its digital twin must show the outward-opening cross-section rather than omitting or reversing it.

The delta -0.30 shape is a design choice for a machine not yet built. Its confinement and stability performance is a prediction to be tested at the confinement gate G1, reported measured-versus-predicted.

title: Centerpost Engineering
lede: The centerpost of the spherical tokamak carries the highest field, current, and neutron load in the machine, making it the hardest component.
body: The core of a spherical tokamak

In a spherical tokamak the central column, the centerpost, is where the toroidal-field conductors pass through the middle of the machine. Because the geometry is compact, this column is slender and carries the most concentrated loads in the entire device: high field, high current, mechanical stress, and neutron flux together.
Magnetic field approaching the 16.84 T peak, with associated Lorentz stress
High current density in the toroidal-field conductors
Neutron loading, since it sits close to the plasma
Thermal loads from resistive and nuclear heating
Why it is the pacing engineering problem

Every advantage of the compact spherical design, high beta, small size, high field, converges as stress in the centerpost. If the centerpost cannot be built to carry these loads reliably, the whole configuration fails. This is why the magnet gate G2 and centerpost design are central to risk retirement.

The centerpost design draws on REBCO high-field magnet practice and structural analysis to carry Lorentz and thermal loads within material limits, with neutron shielding to protect the conductors over the machine's life. Its centerpost lifetime under neutron fluence is one of the flagged engineering questions the program tracks.
The centerpost is a design for a machine not yet built. It is the component the first-of-a-kind unit most needs to validate on hardware.

title: Peak Field 16.84 T
lede: The magnet system is designed for 16.84 T peak field at the conductor with 8 T on axis, the field that makes a compact machine reach gain.
body: The breeder's magnet system is designed for a peak field of 16.84 T at the conductor and 8 T on the plasma axis. Field is what confines the plasma and enables fusion; high field is what lets a compact machine reach the design gain of Q_sci 3.076.

The 16.84 T peak occurs at the conductor, where the field is strongest; the 8 T on-axis value is what the plasma experiences at its center. The gap reflects geometry: field falls off from the coils to the plasma. Both figures matter, the peak sets the engineering limit, the on-axis value sets the plasma physics.
16.84 T requires REBCO high-temperature superconductor at high current density
The field produces large Lorentz forces concentrated in the centerpost
Maintaining superconducting margin and quench protection at this field is hard

The magnet gate G2 exists to prove exactly this: that the coil set reaches and holds 16.84 T peak with 8 T on axis under operational load. Achieving the field is a precondition for plasma operation and for the confinement gate that follows.

16.84 T is a design target for a machine not yet built. It rests on REBCO conductor supply and magnet fabrication meeting their qualification criteria, and it becomes a demonstrated value only when G2 is passed.

title: Plasma Current 9.66 MA
lede: The design plasma current of 9.66 MA sets the confinement and stability the breeder needs to reach its gain point.
body: Plasma current is one of the primary levers on tokamak performance. It sets much of the confinement and helps hold the plasma stable. The breeder is designed for a plasma current of 9.66 MA, chosen together with the field and shape to reach Q_sci 3.076.

Energy confinement in a tokamak scales strongly with plasma current, so 9.66 MA is a large part of why the compact machine can hold enough energy to reach gain. The confinement gate G1 tests whether the real machine, at 9.66 MA and full field, achieves the predicted confinement.
A central solenoid and current-drive capability to establish and sustain 9.66 MA
Stability control to manage a high-current compact plasma
Structural design to handle the forces a large current implies
Interaction with the other design points

9.66 MA does not stand alone. It works with the 8 T on-axis field, the negative triangularity of -0.30, and the compact spherical geometry as one coherent operating point. Change one and the others must move. This is why the design point is quoted as a set, not as isolated numbers.
9.66 MA is a design value for a machine not yet built. First plasma will begin at far lower current, and the ramp to 9.66 MA is where confinement is measured against prediction at G1.

title: The Basis for Q_sci 3.076
lede: The breeder's design gain of Q_sci 3.076 is the ratio of fusion power to plasma heating power that yields the neutron flux the foundry needs.
body: Q_sci is scientific gain: fusion power produced divided by heating power delivered to the plasma. The breeder's design point is Q_sci 3.076, meaning it produces roughly three and a half times the power injected to heat the plasma. This is the gain the foundry needs, and it is a plasma-physics ratio, not a whole-plant one.

The breeder is sized to a supply requirement. Q_sci 3.076 at 85.0 MW fusion power produces the neutron flux needed to breed the target tritium class output and the helium-3 coproduct. A higher gain is not required for the foundry mission, and pursuing it would make the machine larger or harder without serving the product.
8 T on-axis field from the high-field magnet system
9.66 MA plasma current for strong confinement
Negative triangularity of -0.30 for edge and exhaust behavior
Compact spherical geometry for high plasma pressure

Q_sci 3.076 is scientific gain. It is not net electricity and does not imply it, the breeder does not target net electric output. This distinction is central to the whole program: the foundry needs gain, and gain is a lower bar than the net-electric threshold.
Q_sci 3.076 is a design and simulation value for a machine not yet built. It is the headline quantity the confinement gate G1 is built to verify, reported measured-versus-predicted.

title: Fusion Power 85.0 MW
lede: The breeder is designed to produce 85.0 MW of fusion power, the neutron source strength that drives its isotope and irradiation products.
body: The power figure and what it is for

The breeder is designed for 85.0 MW of fusion power. In a foundry this figure matters as a measure of neutron source strength, not as an amount of electricity to sell. 85.0 MW of D-T fusion means a specific rate of 14 MeV neutron production, and that rate is what breeds tritium and serves irradiation.

Fusion power sets the neutron flux; the neutron flux, allocated across the neutron budget, sets the products: the tritium class output near 4 kg/yr, the helium-3 coproduct near 1.97 kg/yr, and neutron-hours for irradiation. 85.0 MW is chosen to supply these, not to reach a power rating.
85.0 MW is fusion power, thermal in origin, not net electrical output
The breeder converts none of it to net grid power by design
The value delivered is the neutron flux and the material it produces

85.0 MW at Q_sci 3.076 follows from the operating point: 8 T on axis, 9.66 MA plasma current, negative triangularity -0.30, in the compact spherical geometry. It is the fusion output of that specific design, not a target set independently.
85.0 MW is a design and simulation value for a machine not yet built. The corresponding neutron yield is what the fuel-loop gate measures against its pre-registered prediction.

title: Tritium Plant Integration
lede: The tritium plant recovers, purifies, stores, and accounts for bred tritium and its helium-3 coproduct, closing the fuel loop.
body: The plant that makes the foundry work

A breeder is only as good as its tritium plant. The plant recovers tritium bred in the blanket, purifies it, returns fuel to the plasma, stores product, and accounts for every gram. It also recovers the helium-3 coproduct. Without an integrated plant, neutrons breed tritium that cannot be captured or sold.
Recovery of tritium from the blanket and plasma exhaust
Isotope separation and purification of the fuel stream
Storage of tritium product and recovery of helium-3
Accountancy: measuring and tracking inventory for product and regulation

The plant is not a bolt-on. It couples to the blanket, the vacuum and pumping systems, and the fueling system, and its design interacts with the breeding ratio lever and the neutron budget. Integration is why the fuel loop is treated as a single gate, G3, rather than as separate plant and blanket tests.

Tritium accountancy is central both to running a foundry and to the byproduct-material licensing basis. The plant must demonstrate that it measures and controls inventory, which is part of the G3 pass criterion and part of the safety case.

The tritium plant is a design for a machine not yet built. Its performance, recovery efficiency and accountancy, is demonstrated at first tritium, where the closed and accounted fuel loop is the proof of the foundry.

title: Blanket and Breeding
lede: The breeding blanket surrounds the plasma, captures 14 MeV neutrons, and converts them to tritium in lithium-bearing material.
body: The breeding blanket is the layer surrounding the plasma that captures fusion neutrons and breeds tritium. When a 14 MeV neutron is absorbed by lithium, it produces tritium and helium. The blanket is where the machine turns neutrons into product, and its design sets the achievable breeding ratio.
Lithium isotopics and lithium-bearing material choice
Neutron multipliers to increase available neutrons for breeding
Blanket thickness and coverage around the plasma
Penetrations for heating, diagnostics, and maintenance that reduce coverage

A one-dimensional calculation of breeding ratio is optimistic. Real blankets have penetrations and structure that absorb neutrons and reduce net breeding. This is why TBR is treated as a lever across 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8, and why the reconciliation between design-level and net three-dimensional breeding is a tracked open question.

Blanket modules experience neutron damage and must be replaceable. The blanket is designed as modules for remote maintenance, which interacts with the assembly sequence and the neutron budget, replaceability requires penetrations, and penetrations cost breeding.

The blanket is a design for a machine not yet built. Its net breeding performance is measured at the fuel-loop gate G3, at first tritium, against the pre-registered prediction for the installed configuration.

title: Vacuum Vessel and Divertor
lede: The vacuum vessel holds the plasma environment and the divertor handles exhaust heat and particles, both shaped by the compact geometry.
body: The vacuum vessel is the sealed chamber that maintains the high vacuum the plasma requires and forms the first structural boundary around it. The divertor is the region that receives plasma exhaust, heat and particles, and channels them away. Both are demanding in a compact, high-power machine.
Maintains operating vacuum with low outgassing
Forms a precision structure sized to the compact spherical geometry
Provides ports for heating, diagnostics, and maintenance access
Carries loads and interfaces with blanket and magnets

Exhaust heat handling is one of the hardest problems in any tokamak. The divertor must accept concentrated heat flux without failing. The negative triangularity of -0.30 is chosen partly to improve exhaust behavior, so the divertor design and the plasma shape are linked decisions.
Why the compact machine makes it harder

Concentrating 85.0 MW of fusion power in a compact machine concentrates the exhaust load. Less surface area is available to spread the heat, which raises the demand on divertor materials and geometry. This is a genuine engineering challenge the design must meet, not assume away.

The vessel and divertor are designs for a machine not yet built. Their performance is verified during commissioning and operation; the vessel is one of the long-lead pacing items that drives the build schedule.

title: Cryogenic Plant
lede: The cryogenic plant keeps the superconducting magnets at operating temperature, a precondition for reaching and holding 16.84 T.
body: The high-field magnets are superconducting, which means they must be held at cryogenic temperature to carry current without resistance. The cryogenic plant provides and maintains that cold environment. If the magnets warm past their margin, they cannot hold 16.84 T and can quench.
Cools the magnets from ambient to operating temperature during commissioning
Maintains temperature and temperature margin during operation
Removes heat loads, including nuclear heating from neutrons near the coils
Supports controlled recovery after any magnet quench

Cryogenic performance is part of magnet commissioning and the magnet gate G2. Verifying temperature margin, how far the conductor sits below its critical temperature, is essential, because margin is what protects the magnet against transient heat and neutron loads at full field.

The cryoplant is a significant utility load and a commissioning-critical system: the magnets cannot be energized until they are cold and stable. Cooldown itself takes time and is an early commissioning stage. The plant's reliability directly affects machine availability, which matters for foundry operation.
The cryogenic plant is a design for a machine not yet built. Its performance is demonstrated during commissioning as a precondition for the magnet gate and all subsequent operation.

title: Power and Magnet Systems
lede: Power systems energize and protect the magnets, drive plasma current, and supply heating, together forming the machine's electrical backbone.
body: The breeder's power and magnet systems energize the superconducting coils, protect them against quench, drive the 9.66 MA plasma current, and supply plasma heating. This is the electrical backbone that turns supplied power into confining field and hot plasma.
Magnet power supplies to energize the toroidal and poloidal field coils
Quench protection to safely dissipate stored energy if a magnet loses superconductivity
Central solenoid and current drive to establish and sustain plasma current
Heating systems to bring the plasma to fusion conditions

A superconducting magnet at 16.84 T stores enormous energy. If part of the coil loses superconductivity (a quench), that energy must be removed safely and fast. Quench protection is therefore a central safety and design function, and demonstrating it is part of the magnet gate G2.

These systems draw substantial power, magnets, current drive, and heating. In a foundry this is acceptable because the machine needs only gain, not net electricity; the recirculating load does not have to be beaten by generated power. This is precisely the threshold the breeder is designed to avoid needing to cross.
The power and magnet systems are designs for a machine not yet built. They are commissioned in stages, with magnet energization and quench protection verified before plasma operation.

title: Remote Maintenance
lede: Neutron-activated components are serviced by remote handling, a design requirement that shapes the blanket, ports, and foundry availability.
body: After operation, components near the plasma are activated by neutrons and cannot be serviced by direct human contact. The breeder is designed for remote maintenance: replacing blanket modules, servicing the divertor, and inspecting internals with remote handling equipment through designed access.
Blanket built as replaceable modules rather than a monolith
Access ports and handling paths designed into the vessel from the start
Component connections designed to be made and broken remotely
Maintenance sequences planned alongside the assembly sequence

A foundry lives on availability, the fraction of time it produces product. Maintenance downtime directly reduces output. Designing for efficient remote maintenance is therefore a foundry requirement, not a convenience: faster module changeouts mean more neutron-hours and more product per year.

Remote maintenance requires access and penetrations, and penetrations reduce blanket coverage and net breeding. This is one of the real trades in the design: maintainability against breeding ratio. It is part of why TBR is treated as a lever rather than a single maximized number.
Remote maintenance is a design requirement for a machine not yet built. Its effectiveness is a major factor in the NOAK and BOAK goal of high, reproducible foundry availability.

title: The Safety Case
lede: The breeder's safety case centers on tritium containment, neutron and activation management, and magnet energy, matched to a byproduct-material framework.
body: A fusion breeder's hazards are specific and bounded: radioactive tritium, neutron activation of materials, and the stored energy in high-field magnets. The safety case addresses these directly. It is not the accident spectrum of a fission core, which is why a byproduct-material framework fits the machine.
Tritium: a radioactive gas requiring containment and accountancy
Neutron activation: components become radioactive and need shielding and handling
Magnet energy: stored energy managed through quench protection
Occupational and public dose around a compact neutron source

Tritium is contained by multiple barriers and tracked by accountancy. Activation is managed by shielding, material choice, and remote maintenance. Magnet energy is handled by quench protection. Dose is managed by shielding and access control. Each hazard has a designed control, and the gates produce evidence, especially G3's tritium accountancy, that supports the case.

A fusion plasma is not a chain reaction; it stops when fueling or heating stops, and it holds very little fuel at any instant. This gives the safety case favorable inherent characteristics, though tritium and activation still require rigorous control and are the focus of the licensing basis.
The safety case is developed for a machine not yet built or licensed, in pre-application engagement with the regulator, with formal submissions governed by counsel review.

title: Tritium Inventory Management
lede: Every gram of tritium is measured, tracked, and accounted for, a requirement for both foundry operation and the licensing basis.
body: Tritium is both the breeder's product and a regulated radioactive material, so it must be measured and tracked continuously. Inventory management covers how much tritium exists, where it is in the plant, and how it moves, from breeding in the blanket to storage as product.
Product: the tritium class output near 4 kg/yr must be quantified to be sold
Regulation: the byproduct-material safety case requires demonstrated accountancy
Safety: containment depends on knowing inventory and detecting loss
Fuel cycle: the plasma is refueled from recovered tritium, so tracking closes the loop

Inventory is measured across the plant, recovery, purification, storage, and fueling, so that the total is known and reconciled. Discrepancies signal either measurement error or loss, both of which matter. This accountancy is part of the fuel-loop gate G3, where the closed and accounted loop is the pass criterion.
Because tritium decays to helium-3, inventory management also tracks the helium-3 coproduct near 1.97 kg/yr. The two are accounted together as products of the same fuel cycle.

Tritium inventory management is a design and procedural requirement for a machine not yet built. Demonstrating it on hardware, at first tritium, is inseparable from proving the foundry function itself.

title: Neutron Shielding
lede: Shielding confines 14 MeV neutrons, protects the magnets and workers, and manages activation, shaping the facility layout.
body: D-T fusion produces energetic 14 MeV neutrons. These neutrons are the product, but outside the blanket they are a hazard: they activate materials, damage the magnets, and pose a dose risk. Shielding is how the machine confines and manages them, and it drives much of the facility design.
Protect the superconducting magnets from neutron damage and heating
Reduce activation of surrounding structure and equipment
Limit worker and public dose around the facility
Preserve the neutron budget by directing neutrons to the blanket, not losing them

The centerpost and coils sit close to the plasma in a compact machine, so shielding the magnets is critical to their lifetime. Neutron fluence on the conductors is a flagged engineering question, and shielding is the primary defense that keeps the magnets viable over the machine's operating life.

Shielding is heavy and voluminous, so it sets the building layout, the siting footprint, and the maintenance access design. It interacts with the assembly sequence, shielding structure is among the first things built, and with remote maintenance, since shielded components must still be accessible.
The shielding plan is a design for a machine not yet built. Its adequacy is verified through analysis and, ultimately, by measured dose and activation during commissioning and operation.

title: Instrumentation and Diagnostics
lede: The first-of-a-kind unit is heavily instrumented so that every gate is measured against prediction and every anomaly is understood.
body: A first-of-a-kind machine exists to be measured. Instrumentation and diagnostics let the program observe plasma behavior, magnet performance, neutron production, and tritium inventory in enough detail to compare hardware to prediction and to diagnose whatever the machine does that the design did not expect.
Plasma: current, density, temperature, confinement, and stability
Magnets: field, temperature margin, strain, and quench signals
Neutrons: yield and spectrum, tied to fusion power and breeding
Tritium: inventory and flows through the fuel loop

Each physics gate depends on diagnostics: G1 on confinement measurement, G2 on field and margin measurement, G3 on neutron and tritium measurement. Without adequate diagnostics a gate cannot be judged, so diagnostic coverage is part of the gate design, not an afterthought.

FOAK carries more instrumentation than a production foundry unit would need, because its job is to learn. Some diagnostics will prove essential and carry forward to NOAK; others will prove unnecessary and be removed. Deciding which is one of FOAK's outputs to the manufacturing plan.
The diagnostic suite is a design for a machine not yet built. It is what turns the first build from a demonstration into a measured, reportable body of evidence against pre-registered predictions.

title: From Simulation to Hardware
lede: The breeder's design is a body of simulation that the built machine will validate gate by gate, measured against pre-registered predictions.
body: Today the breeder exists as simulation: plasma physics models, magnet and structural analysis, and neutronics for breeding. Validation is the process of comparing what these models predict to what the built machine actually does. The gate program is the structure of that comparison.
Confinement models validated at G1 against measured energy confinement
Magnet and structural models validated at G2 against measured field and margin
Neutronics and breeding models validated at G3 against measured yield and TBR

Simulation bounds behavior but cannot settle it, especially for confinement scaling and three-dimensional net breeding, where the gap between model and reality is a known risk. Only the hardware settles these. This is why the program does not present simulation results as achievements, and why it builds a first-of-a-kind unit at all.

Validation is reported measured-versus-predicted, using the pre-registered predictions. A model that predicted the machine well is validated; one that missed is corrected and feeds the NOAK design. Either outcome advances the program, which is why the discipline matters more than any single number matching.
All current figures are simulation-based design values for a machine not yet built. Validation converts them, one gate at a time, into demonstrated results.

title: The Digital Twin
lede: A digital twin mirrors the design and, in time, the built machine, linking simulation to measured behavior for design and validation.
body: A digital twin is a detailed computational model of the machine that runs alongside the physical program. In the design phase it embodies the frozen physics, Q_sci 3.076, 85.0 MW, 9.66 MA, 16.84 T, negative triangularity -0.30, so the design can be explored and interrogated. Once hardware exists, the twin is updated against measured behavior.
Represent the frozen design point consistently across the program
Explore operating scenarios and sensitivities before hardware exists
Compare predicted behavior to measured results at each gate
Carry lessons from FOAK forward into NOAK design

A digital twin is only as good as its physics and its correspondence to reality. During the design phase the twin is a simulation, not evidence of performance. Its representations, including plasma shape, must match the canonical design; for example the negative triangularity must be shown correctly as an outward-opening plasma, not omitted or reversed.

As gates are passed, measured data refines the twin, and the refined twin improves predictions for later units. This closes the loop between simulation and hardware described in the validation program, and it is where the twin earns its keep, by improving as the machine teaches it.
The digital twin models a machine not yet built. It is a design and analysis tool, and its outputs are design values until validated against hardware at the gates.

title: Quality Assurance
lede: Quality assurance runs from conductor qualification through assembly and commissioning, so the built machine matches the design that was analyzed.
body: A design is only meaningful if the built machine matches it. Quality assurance is the discipline that keeps fabrication, assembly, and commissioning true to the analyzed design, so that when the machine is measured at the gates, it is the designed machine being tested and not an unintended variant.
Conductor: REBCO tape qualified against current-density and defect criteria
Fabrication: coils, vessel, and blanket built to tolerance
Assembly: components installed correctly and in sequence
Commissioning: subsystems verified before and during bring-up
Why it matters for the gates

If a magnet falls short of 16.84 T, QA records must show whether it was designed short, built short, or damaged, otherwise a gate miss cannot be diagnosed. QA makes the pre-registered comparison meaningful by ensuring deviations are traceable to a cause. It is the record that lets a miss teach something.

QA data from FOAK, which tolerances were hard to hold, which steps introduced defects, feeds directly into the manufacturing plan for NOAK and BOAK. Quality assurance is therefore both a control on the first build and an input to standardizing the later ones.
The QA program governs a machine not yet built. Its purpose is to ensure that the design and simulation values, once tested on hardware, are tested on the machine that was actually intended.

title: Commissioning Gates vs Physics Gates
lede: Commissioning milestones prove subsystems work; the physics gates prove the machine performs, and the two are kept distinct.
body: It is easy to confuse getting a machine running with proving it performs. The program keeps them separate. Commissioning milestones confirm that subsystems function, vacuum, cryogenics, magnet energization, first plasma. The physics gates (G1, G2, G3) confirm that the machine meets its design point and breeds tritium.
Magnets reach operating temperature with margin
First plasma is formed and controlled
G1: confinement sufficient to reach Q_sci 3.076
G2: 16.84 T peak field held under load
G3: neutrons breed and are accounted as tritium

A machine can pass commissioning, everything switches on, and still fall short at a physics gate, for instance if confinement is below prediction. Treating first plasma or magnet energization as if it were proof of performance would overclaim. The gates, reported against pre-registered predictions, are the real evidence; commissioning is the necessary precondition, not the demonstration itself.
